questions.q: State the relationship between the areas of the three squares in the visual proof of the Pythagoras theorem.
questions.a: The area of the square on the hypotenuse (c²) equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides (a² + b²). A wrong answer (e.g., saying the areas are equal or subtracting) reveals the student has not grasped the core area-conservation principle of the proof.

questions.q: In the classic square-within-a-square proof, why must the four triangles used in both arrangements be congruent?
questions.a: The four triangles are congruent because they are all right triangles with legs a and b (same shape and size). Congruence ensures they have equal area, so subtracting their total area from the large square (a+b)² leaves a consistent comparison. If a student says "they look similar" or "they are all right triangles" without specifying equal legs, they miss the precise condition for equal area subtraction.

questions.q: A right triangle has legs of length 6 cm and 8 cm. Using the visual proof idea, what is the area of the square on the hypotenuse? Show the steps by computing the areas of the two smaller squares and adding them.
questions.a:
Step 1: Area of square on side 6 cm = 6² = 36 cm².
Step 2: Area of square on side 8 cm = 8² = 64 cm².
Step 3: Sum of areas = 36 + 64 = 100 cm².
Step 4: By the theorem, this equals the area of the square on the hypotenuse, so c² = 100 cm².
A wrong answer (e.g., 14 cm² or 48 cm²) shows the student is adding side lengths instead of areas, or multiplying legs instead of squaring.

questions.q: Compare the square-within-a-square proof and the rearrangement proof (where triangles are moved to form two rectangles). What is the common geometric principle that makes both proofs valid?
questions.a: Both proofs rely on the principle of area conservation: when shapes are dissected and rearranged without overlap or gaps, the total area remains unchanged. A student who only describes the visual differences without naming area conservation is focusing on appearance rather than the underlying mathematical invariant.

questions.q: A student claims the visual proof only works for the 3-4-5 triangle because the squares have integer sides. Evaluate this claim and explain why it is correct or incorrect.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect. The visual proof uses arbitrary lengths a and b; the dissection works for any positive real numbers because congruence and area addition hold generally, not just for integers. If a student agrees with the claim, they confuse a specific numerical example with a general geometric proof.

questions.q: Create your own visual proof idea for the Pythagoras theorem using a different large shape (not a square of side a+b). Sketch the concept and describe the area equivalence in words.
questions.a: A good answer might use a rectangle of dimensions (a+b) by c, or a trapezoid, showing that the total area can be expressed in two ways leading to a²+b²=c². The key is a clear description of two area decompositions of the same shape. A poor answer simply redraws the standard square proof or fails to show two distinct area expressions.
